title: Onprem cluster drift and handoff guidance
content:
Purpose:
This note is a short, pragmatic guidance for field engineers and platform owners when handing off an on-prem Kubernetes cluster (mixed bare-metal + vSphere) and for detecting/repairing configuration drift during upgrades. It collects: quick checks, Terraform module call patterns we use, safe upgrade sequence, common drift signatures, and an emergency rollback checklist.

Context and scope:
- Target clusters: customer-managed on-prem clusters we deploy through our Private package (VPC-less or connected VPC), typically a control-plane on vSphere and worker pools that may be bare-metal or vSphere VMs.
- Installer model: we push infrastructure via our terraform modules, ignition/user-data for OS, and a lightweight operator (cluster-agent) for day-2 tasks.
- This is a working note: expect rough TODOs and hyperlinks to tickets. Use Confluence or the cluster runbook for final vendor-approved steps.

Quick handoff checklist (for SRE -> Field/CS handoff):
- Deliverables to handoff: terraform state snapshot (s3 object or local state copy), kubeconfig with expiring token + instructions to rotate, KMS key identifiers for secrets, platform contact list.
- Operational health: control-plane ready (>3 masters or HA pair configured), etcd snapshot date within last 7 days, system namespaces in Ready state, < 5% node NotReady in past 24h.
- Access & credentials: verify SSH jump host config, confirm IPMI/BMC creds for bare-metal nodes are stored in vault path, verify KMS/HSM access for encryption-at-rest keys.
- Network and DNS: confirm BGP or static routes for pod/cluster CIDRs, DNS glue records for api.<cluster> and external-apis.
- Monitoring hooks: metrics endpoints available (node-exporter, kube-state-metrics), alerting configured in pagerduty.

Terraform module notes (common patterns & pitfalls):
- Module inputs we rely on most: control_plane_count, node_pool_profiles (cpu,gpu,replicas), bootstrap_image_id, ipmi_credentials_secret_path, pxe_boot_script_url, vcenter_cluster, datastore, network_portgroup. Keep these inputs in the cluster-specific var file.
- State handling: always lock remote state (s3 + dynamodb or GCS + locking) before plan/apply. For on-prem: we use a namespaced S3 bucket with lifecycle rules.
- Immutable node pools: prefer creating new node pool + cordon/drain approach during major kube upgrades instead of in-place kubelet binary updates on bare-metal. This avoids drift where OS level packages differ.
- Edge-case: vSphere template drift. If upgrades replace template in-place, you can end up with VMs with mixed cloud-init user-data versions. Best practice: create a new template version, reference by template_version tag in TF, then roll nodes.
- Example minimal var snippet (conceptual):
  - cluster_name: "acme-prod-nyc"
  - control_plane_count: "3"
  - node_pool_profiles: "[{\"name\":\"compute-gpu\",\"replicas\":8,\"instance_profile\":\"ibm-p451\"}]"
  - ipmi_credentials_secret_path: "vault://secret/onprem/acme/ipmi"
  - pxe_boot_script_url: "https://assets.redwood-inference.com/pxe/bootstrap-v2.sh"

Drift detection heuristics (how we detect things that differ from TF state):
- Drift type: OS image digest mismatch. Detection: check image ID/annotation on nodes vs expected template_id in terraform state. Symptom: kubelet restarts, certificates mismatched.
- Drift type: Kernel param/disallowed sysctl. Detection: compare /proc/sys values to terraform-provisioned expected set (we record expected sysctls in configmap infra-metadata). Symptom: networking flaps, kube-proxy errors.
- Drift type: Network route differences (BGP next-hop changes). Detection: routing table snapshot vs last-known snapshot in state bucket. Symptom: pods unreachable across racks.
- Drift type: Etcd size or member list mismatch (manual add/remove). Detection: etcdctl member list vs terraform resources. Symptom: split-brain alerts.

Repair approaches (order matters):
1) Non-destructive reconciliation: attempt to bring nodes into compliance using the cluster-agent (re-run provisioner, push expected sysctls, restart kubelet).
2) Terraform import + plan: if resources were created manually (new ipmi entry, new VM), import into state and run plan to converge.
3) Replace nodes: for node-level drift (images, kernel), create new node pool and cordon/drain the old nodes. This is safest for bare-metal if you have spare capacity.
4) Control-plane restore: if etcd is inconsistent and automated repair won't cut it, restore etcd from last healthy snapshot (document exact snapshot id and restoration steps).

Upgrade sequencing (minor vs major):
- Minor patches (x.y.z -> x.y.z+N): can be done in-place with rolling upgrades. Sequence: control-plane masters staggered with leader election verification, then node pools with pod disruption budgets honored.
- Minor version bumps (1.x -> 1.x+1): use kubeadm or our operator-based upgrade to update apiserver/etcd first, then kubelet on nodes. For bare-metal nodes, prefer new node pool creation if kernel changes are included in the kubelet packaging.
- Major upgrades (1.x -> 1.x+1 breaking): schedule a maintenance window, take etcd snapshot, test upgrade on a staging clone (see cloning notes below), then follow the operator canary rollout (canary master, canary node pool), then full rollout.

Cloning a cluster for safe upgrade testing (quick recipe):
- Snapshot terraform state, copy relevant vSphere templates or bare-metal provisioning scripts to a sandbox project.
- Point terraform variables at a sandbox namespace (unique CIDRs, DNS entries).
- Restore etcd to sandbox cluster or run a seed dataset job to create test workloads.
- Run the planned upgrade on sandbox, observe metrics and run our standard smoke tests (latency, e2e job pass/fail).

Emergency rollback checklist (if upgrade causes regressions):
- Immediately scale down new node pools and scale up previous node pools (if you used blue/green or immutable nodes).
- If control-plane regressed: restore etcd from snapshot (documented S3 path + snapshot id), reinstate previous API server flags by reverting to older manifest in static-manifests-backups.
- Rotate client certificates if leaked during the window.
- Capture forensic logs: journalctl for kubelet, kube-apiserver logs, kube-controller-manager logs, and upload to secure bucket for post-mortem.

Handoff notes for field technicians (practical tips):
- When you arrive on-site: confirm IPMI reachability and that power profiles are nominal. If IPMI unreachable, escalate to network team before touching nodes.
- Serial console: always use serial over vSphere console for initial debug (avoids GUI timeouts).
- Safe reboot: drain node first with kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data then power-cycle via IPMI.
- When replacing a broken physical node: ensure MAC addresses and BMC credentials are updated in terraform vars, and tag the new hardware with the same rack/zone metadata.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we automatically tag node pools with the last-applied-terraform-version in a node label? That would make drift detection trivial. (Ticket: JIRA-OPS-4021).
- Investigate adding an automated snapshot/compare tool for /proc/sys and image digests pushed to the state bucket nightly.
- Draft a small k8s admission plugin to block nodes with kernel parameters outside of an allowlist.

References and quick links:
- Confluence runbook: CONFLUENCE-1234 (detailed cluster lifecycle)
- Terraform modules repo: github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules (see modules/onprem-vsphere, modules/baremetal)
- Upgrade playbook canonical doc: CONFLUENCE-UPGRADE-PLAYBOOK (link in Confluence)
- Last done: upgrade for acme-prod-nyc (JIRA ticket: JIRA-OPS-3987)

Notes to self: keep this doc short and add a small checklist card to the console's cluster detail page with the critical files: latest etcd snapshot id, terraform state id, bootstrap-image-id.

— Asha
